What do you consider to be "organic storytelling" in video games?

I'd say when the game does a good job of transitioning between gameplay and cinematics (or cinematic like gameplay) that it doesn't break the immersion you have while playing the character.

I think the Half Life games did a good job of this, it was more cinematic gameplay, since you always had control of your character to a certain degree. There were times when you could move around freely while the story happened around you and other times when you were prevented from moving around, but you could still look around. You always felt like the story was happening to you, rather than suddenly getting jolted by the game switching the perspective completely around, so it always flows very naturally.

Not exactly what you mean but I did like the effort MGS4 sometimes went into for ending a cutscene by moving the camera naturally into the default camera position. It's something more games have gotten into the habit of doing but I remember thinking it was done rather well in MGS4.

Though, more similarly, I dislike the habit of having cutscenes play out behind a window (Bioshock and Dead Space come to mind). It felt very unnatural. I don't think games do it so much any more.

To me it is when the game mechanics and story intertwine nicely. Such as in Braid, during the last level using the main ability of the game (rewind) shows what is actually the right time chronology of the story and... mind blown. In Rayman Origins, during the game you collect those little light creatures named Lums while the Magician gets really crazy about them. Towards the end, you start seeing them used as light bulbs or to power machinery...

In Left 4 Dead, there are no transitions nor cutscenes but the story of the places is told through graffiti and the personality of the characters through banter. It feels very natural.

Braid

Eh. I liked the ending to it, but in terms of the whole scope of the game, it felt like there was barely a story at all. And knowing the dev (who's super douchey), it feels like he tacked on a 'story' that can't really be explained. That way he can treat anyone who brings it up like uneducated plebs.

And Aquaria did a more interesting version of the 'cyclical storyline' motif a year before Braid did.
Same, I did not like the rest of the so-called "story". Just the brilliant last level that can be taken independently from the rest of the game, and I am very glad to have experienced it.

I feel that a game such as Europa Universalis has organic storytelling. An alternate world history unfolds and you watch and take part it as it happens.

I also have to agree with Brock, FROM games since Demon's Souls have done this wonderfully. The player is invited to cobble up an understanding of past events from little in-world details and item descriptions.
